items.title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render

items.title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
items.text: The 's function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous -then- pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race.Workflow SDKstart()getHookByToken()start() The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving to .resumeHookcreateHook({ token })getConflict()null The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate throws carrying the owner's and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally.start()HookConflictErrorconflictingRunId Setting keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from , so late duplicates are still ref

items.title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
items.text: Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems. You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time. We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying. Schedules builds on the static approach used by , but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Once enabled, every push to a connected GitHub repository is automatically reviewed for vulnerabilities, and findings are reported in the .Vercel Security ReviewVulnerabilities dashboard Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, direct and force pushes to your production branch are reviewed as well. Every project affected by a single push is reviewed together. Each finding records the project, environment, branch, and commit, with a summary, a suggested fix, and an AI-generated severity rating. Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. When there's a pull request, it also posts findings as review comments that link back to each finding. On public repositories, finding details stay in the dashboard. Clicking on a vulnerability report hands the finding to Vercel Agent, which proposes a fix and opens a pull request for you to review. items.title: Vercel MCP now supports Client ID Metadata Documents
items.text: Any MCP client can now ask to connect to . You still log in and approve each connection, but the client no longer has to be reviewed by Vercel first. Previously, Vercel reviewed and allowlisted each client and its redirect URIs by hand, and anything not on the list was rejected.Vercel MCP To connect, a client publishes a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), a JSON file on its own domain that describes it, and uses that file's HTTPS URL as its OAuth . This follows the MCP authorization spec, which now recommends CIMD over Dynamic Client Registration.client_id Because Vercel hasn't reviewed these clients, the consent screen shows where each one comes from: its name, its logo, and the hostname that serves its metadata document, for example "Claude Code by claude.ai". CIMD clients don't get the Vercel verified badge, so the hostname is what you're trusting when you approve. Apps already registered with Vercel are unchanged. Read the to connect your client.Vercel MCP documentation Read more

items.title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
items.text: Today, we are launching in public beta.Vercel Security Review Security Review is a new capability in , alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories.Vercel Agent Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings. Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works: Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment. The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. items.title: Free Certified Patch for Critical Rails Active Storage Vulnerability
items.text: Ruby on Rails has released security updates addressing 21 vulnerabilities, including a critical Active Storage flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files to a server through crafted uploads. Under certain configurations, attackers may also be able to read sensitive files, potentially leading to remote code execution. Socket is releasing a free Certified Patch for the critical vulnerability, tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 (CVSS 9.8). The patch is available to everyone, including developers and organizations that are not Socket customers, providing an additional remediation option for teams that cannot immediately upgrade Rails. Impact # The vulnerability affects Rails applications that use ImageMagick to process Active Storage attachments. ImageMagick supports multiple file format handlers, known as coders, some of which can access files outside the uploaded image. Active Storage did not restrict these coders, potentially allowing an attacker to invoke dangerous operations through a crafted upload. Active Storage automatically analyzes files when they are attached, so exploitation does not require a separate preview, image transformation, or explicit an

items.title: Shai-Hulud Descendant Surfaces in Malicious Ruby Gem That Steals Credentials and Poisons AI Tools
items.text: Socket’s Threat Research Team analyzed strutil-core version 1.0.1, a malicious RubyGems package that runs a 5.48 MB credential-stealing worm when it is installed. The RubyGems account jamnajiea published a clean 1.0.0 on November 1, 2026, and pushed the malicious 1.0.1 less than two hours later. Socket’s AI Scanner flagged it 70 seconds after publication, and RubyGems removed both versions about five hours after the malicious release. strutil-core was a standalone gem, not a compromised existing package. We found no public projects that depended on it, and we have not confirmed any victims or any packages the worm infected from it. The payload is what makes it worth a closer look. It is a new build of the testmetest worm, a member of the Miasma family that grew out of the publicly released Shai-Hulud toolkit, and strutil-core is the only RubyGems package we have tied to it. Bitbison’s sandbox run confirms that the gem runs the payload at install time and reads credential files. The rest of this post comes from static analysis of the code, not from activity seen on victim systems. Install-time execution: a native extension script, ext/strutil-core/extconf.rb, downloads the Bun JavaS

items.title: GitHub to Block pull_request_target Workflows by Default Starting December 2
items.text: GitHub will begin blocking GitHub Actions workflows triggered by pull_request_target in public repositories on December 2, 2026, expanding its protections against a class of CI/CD vulnerabilities that has repeatedly enabled attackers to steal credentials and compromise open source software releases. The restriction, originally announced in September, will prevent affected workflows from running unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them. GitHub had initially scheduled enforcement for November 2 but confirmed the postponed December 2 deadline in a new update this week, giving maintainers additional time to review their automation and configure exceptions. The new restriction goes beyond protections introduced in June, when GitHub updated actions/checkout to prevent common attempts to check out untrusted pull request code inside privileged workflows. This time, GitHub is blocking the pull_request_target trigger itself by default, including for workflows that use it safely. pull_request_target Is Now a Common Attack Vector Vector # GitHub introduced pull_request_target in 2020 to help maintainers automate tasks involving pull requests from external contributors.

items.title: Hardening GitHub Actions Against Outside Threats
items.text: The supply chain attacks that defined 2025 and 2026 did not arrive as typosquats or as newly published malicious packages. They arrived inside legitimate, widely installed packages whose maintainers wrote no malicious code. The malicious code entered during the release, and in most cases the release ran on GitHub Actions. Some of the better-known incidents on widely used projects, as a sample rather than a complete list: tj-actions/changed-files, March 2025 Nx s1ngularity, August 2025 Shai-Hulud, from September 2025 trivy-action, March 2026 axios, March 2026 TanStack Router, May 2026 GhostAction, across 2025 and 2026 LiteLLM 1.107.0, October 2026 A recurring pattern was compromise of the release process or its credentials. In some incidents, attackers made the project's own automation build and ship the malicious artifact, as in Ultralytics and TanStack Router. In others, they stole publishing credentials from that automation and published directly—Nx's postmortem explicitly states that the malicious packages did not originate from its CI pipeline. items.title: Composer 2.11 Adds Dependency Cooldowns
items.text: Composer 2.11 has introduced dependency cooldowns, giving PHP developers a native way to delay newly published package versions before they become eligible for installation. The release arrives nearly a year after developers first requested the feature, bringing Composer into line with package managers that have already adopted minimum release age policies to reduce exposure to supply chain attacks. The new config.policy.cooldown setting allows developers to specify a waiting period in hours, days, or weeks. It is disabled by default and applies during dependency resolution, including composer update and composer require. Existing lockfile installations remain unaffected. The feature also supports organization-wide configuration through Private Packagist, which can enforce cooldowns regardless of the Composer version developers and CI systems are running. Preventing Cooldown Bypasses # The original GitHub issue opened in November 2025 and gained urgency following a series of high-profile supply chain compromises.
